title: Capacity is a token budget
summary: A load-balancer metric can improve while service collapses, because a token budget and a request count measure different things.

steps.title: 8% long-context share: the usual baseline
body: The long mode averages 24,000 prompt tokens against 1,200 for the short mode. At an 8% long share: goodput 18,127 tok/s, first-token p99 3,859 ms, attainment 97.0%, load spread 0.33.
This is the same fleet setup used in the routing and chunking findings. Nothing here is broken yet.
steps.look_for: A moderate, steady load spread around 0.33 in the Machine level tab.

steps.title: 0% long: the best case in the sweep
body: With no long-context requests at all: goodput 19,037 tok/s, first-token p99 just 407 ms, attainment 100.0%, load spread 0.38.
First-token latency is nearly ten times better than at 8% long share. One long request changes the picture far more than its share of the request count suggests.
steps.look_for: First-token p99 dropping to under half a second.

steps.title: 16% long: load spread is already falling
body: At 16% long share: goodput 16,748 tok/s, first-token p99 5,033 ms, attainment 93.6%, load spread 0.28 — lower than at 8%, even though service is getting worse.
The balancer looks like it is doing a better job precisely as service starts to fall apart, because a few enormous requests make every replica uniformly saturated.
steps.look_for: The imbalance coefficient of variation reading better than the 8% run despite lower attainment.

steps.title: 32% long: load spread keeps improving while goodput halves
body: At 32% long share: load spread falls to 0.24 — the best-looking number in the whole sweep — while goodput drops to 8,515 tok/s (less than half of the 8% baseline) and first-token p99 rises to 13,824 ms, 34 times worse. Attainment is 64.9%.

One 24,000-token context consumes what eight chat turns consume, so raising the long share consumes admission capacity that a request count would have said was free. Open the A/B view with A = 8% and B = 32% long share.
steps.look_for: A dashboard watching only imbalance would report improvement through this entire step.

steps.title: The token-denomination argument
body: At 32% long share the fleet is at 30% of its rated request rate and still produces a 13.8 second first-token tail. A system that counts requests cannot see this happening.
This is the clearest case in this project for denominating capacity, rate limits and routing signals in tokens rather than requests.
steps.look_for: The token-based capacity gauge in the Cluster tab against the request-count gauge beside it.
